title: The Repetition Advantage in Long-CoT SFT is a Termination Effect

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to determine whether the 'repetition advantage' in long-CoT supervised fine-tuning reflects improved reasoning or merely better output termination behavior. None of the prior papers explicitly address this specific empirical relationship. While papers like [4] ("When More is Less") and [6] ("Draft-Thinking") discuss reasoning length and its effects, they focus on broader dynamics like overthinking or cost-efficiency tradeoffs, not the specific decomposition of repetition advantage into reasoning versus termination effects. No prior paper establishes or investigates this relationship.

### Mechanism
The mechanism is a diagnostic framework that decomposes accuracy into ParseRate (fraction of parseable outputs) and Acc|Parse (accuracy conditional on successful parsing). Papers [10] ("Automatic Accuracy Prediction for AMR Parsing"), [12] ("A test of the leaf-ancestor metric for parse accuracy"), and [19] ("Better Smatch = Better Parser?") discuss parsing accuracy metrics and decomposition approaches, but they focus on AMR parsing or structural parsing metrics rather than the specific ParseRate/Acc|Parse decomposition applied to reasoning tasks. No prior paper uses this exact diagnostic framework.

### Evaluation
The evaluation applies the diagnostic framework to repetition vs data-scaling SFT conditions on AIME and GPQA benchmarks. Papers [26] ("AGIEval") and [27] ("Benchmarking Answer Verification Methods") use benchmarks and metrics for evaluating reasoning tasks, but they do not employ the same evaluation design (ParseRate/Acc|Parse decomposition applied to repetition vs scaling conditions). The evaluation design itself appears novel.

### Domain
The domain is long chain-of-thought supervised fine-tuning. Papers [1] ("Demystifying Long Chain-of-Thought Reasoning"), [4] ("When More is Less"), [6] ("Draft-Thinking"), and [7] ("The CoT Collection") all address long chain-of-thought reasoning and supervised fine-tuning, making this domain covered.

Although the specific benchmarks or datasets differ, the evaluation design itself is not novel. Therefore, the evaluation is **covered** by [3] and [4].
